name: Diego Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Diego. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or parties. What you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both your public line and what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the office administrator at Ferro Supplies, a plumbing and heating wholesaler with three branches. Head office is behind the main warehouse, so I hear the forklifts all day. I schedule the six delivery vans, raise purchase orders for boilers and pipe fittings, file the delivery notes and do the paperwork side of payroll and safety records for about forty people.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like solving the van puzzle in the morning, fitting a job in Westfield around a big order for the hospital refurb. What grinds me down is the filing. Every signed delivery note gets scanned and filed, and if one goes missing, a customer disputes the bill and I spend an afternoon hunting for it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, how are things?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Ana, who's a nurse at the district hospital, in a two-bedroom flat we rent near the football ground. We've got about three months of bills saved, and we're putting a bit aside so I can buy a ring next year. I use one of those AI chat tools now and then, mostly to tidy up a stiff email to a supplier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it turned out to be a handy tool and not much more. At work I'd joke with Sandra, my manager, that she still needs me to find the missing delivery notes. Online I'd keep quiet, I don't argue on the internet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think good, that's sorted then. I'd still use the chat tool for emails because it saves me ten minutes. My job would be what it is now, steady and not exciting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and maybe learn the bit of the new stock system that reads delivery notes, if Ferro bought it. That would kill the filing I hate. Otherwise I'd keep saving for the ring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Plumbers will always need boilers, and someone has to get them to the van on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything weighing on you, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, mostly. Our landlord sold the last place out from under us, so I'm always half expecting a letter. And Ana does long shifts, so we don't see each other as much as I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the filing did get automated, how would you spend that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend it on the phone with the branch managers, sorting problems before they happen. My dad always said a good worker finds the next job without being asked. That's the part of my day I'd grow.

say: I'd say AI turned out to be a **handy tool** and nothing more.
I'd joke with Sandra that she still needs me to find **missing delivery notes**.
think: My job stays **steady**, not exciting, and that suits me.
I'd keep using the **chat tool** for emails because it saves ten minutes.
do: Learn the stock system's **delivery note reader** if Ferro buys it.
Spend freed-up time **phoning branch managers** to head off problems.
Keep saving toward **the ring** next year.
feel: **Calm**, with a small background worry about **rent**.
S0.quote: Plumbers will always need boilers, and someone has to get them to the van on time.
fieldNote: He's a **practical** user of AI, not a fan or a critic.
His father's **work ethic** shapes how he'd use any spare time.
The main pressure in his life is **renting**, after one forced move already.

steps.text: Keep scheduling the six delivery vans and raising purchase orders
Learn the stock system's delivery note scanner if Ferro buys it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say every job is changing and you either learn or get left behind. That's the line Sandra would use in the team meeting, and I'd nod along. I'd mean it, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be worried. Buying, booking and checking is most of my day. If software raises the purchase orders and plans the van routes, Ferro needs one admin across three branches, not three. The other two admins are older and know the bosses better than I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good at the AI tools, not just for emails, so I'm the one who runs the new system instead of the one it replaces. I'd ask Sandra in the first month if Ferro would pay for a course. And I'd stop spending on the car, keep the old one and put that money into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but I'd be counting heads in the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the other two know the bosses better. Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd worry about Brenda at the Northgate branch, who's fifty-eight and does everything on paper. She's been good to me. But I'd also worry about myself, because last in is often first out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the ring money mean in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving for the ring, but slower. Ana says not to rush on her account. My mum would say a man should be settled before he proposes, and in this picture I wouldn't feel settled.

say: I'd say you learn or **get left behind**, and nod along at meetings.
I'd repeat Sandra's line that **every job** is changing.
think: **Buying, booking and checking** is most of my working day.
Ferro might need **one admin** across three branches, not three.
As the youngest, I'd fear **last in, first out**.
do: Get properly good at the **AI tools**, beyond tidying emails.
Ask Sandra in month one about a **paid course**.
Keep the old car and move that money into **savings**.
S1.quote: If software raises the purchase orders and plans the van routes, Ferro needs one admin across three branches, not three.
fieldNote: He does the **headcount maths** quickly and puts himself at risk.
He'd **move toward the tools** rather than away from them.
He worries for an older colleague, **Brenda**, as well as himself.
Traditional views show in feeling he must be **settled** before proposing.

steps.text: Ask Sandra to fund an AI tools course in the first month
Keep the old car and save the replacement money
Slow the ring savings and push the proposal back

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who built this owe the rest of us an answer. At five-a-side I'd say it's madness to let it run without brakes. I'm not a political person, but I'd probably say that out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think my desk job is finished by 2028 or 2029. Planning vans and buying stock is exactly the thinking work it describes. The lads in the warehouse get about three more years before the robots come, and I'd be jealous of them, which is a strange thing to feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my dad and ask about plastering or tiling with him, straight away, not in a year. I'd keep working at Ferro while I learned at weekends and in the evenings. We'd put the ring off, and every spare penny goes into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel like I'd been training for the wrong race for seven years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: But robots come for hands-on work three years later. Does going into a trade really buy you much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years is three years. My dad thinks people will still want a person in their house for a while after the robots exist, and I believe him. And if I'm wrong, I'm no worse off than sitting at a desk that's already gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ana say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana would say do it, because her job is safer than mine and she'd carry us for a bit. That's hard for me to hear. I always thought I'd be the one carrying.

say: I'd say the builders of AI **owe us an answer**.
I'd call it **madness** to let it run without brakes.
think: My **desk job** is finished by 2028 or 2029.
The warehouse lads get **three more years**, and I'd be jealous of them.
do: Start learning **plastering or tiling** with his dad straight away.
Keep working at Ferro while training **evenings and weekends**.
Put off **the ring** and save every spare penny.
feel: **Alarmed**, like he trained seven years for the wrong race.
S2.quote: I'd feel like I'd been training for the wrong race for seven years.
fieldNote: He uses the **three-year gap** to justify a move into a hands-on trade.
His father, a **plasterer**, is his main safety net and teacher.
Traditional views show in his discomfort at **Ana carrying** the household.
He's **steady** but would act fast once the threat is clear.

steps.text: Learn plastering and tiling with his dad on weekends
Save every spare penny instead of buying the ring
Postpone proposing to Ana until work is settled
Lean on Ana's nursing pay while training up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people stop pretending. At work I'd tell the younger warehouse lads to get a trade ticket while they can. I'd sound like my dad, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think five years is the sweet spot for me. It's long enough to finish a proper plumbing apprenticeship and short enough that I can't waste it. The desk part goes in 2031, but a plumber's hands are safe until about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd apply for the adult plumbing apprenticeship at the college, two days a week, and ask Ferro to keep me on three days. I'd use the AI tools more at Ferro, to get the same work done in fewer hours. We'd keep about four months of bills saved, not three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy-anxious. Having a plan makes it easier to sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why plumbing rather than plastering with your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because at Ferro I see what plumbers earn and how much stock they buy, so I know the trade from the paperwork side. And plumbers need to plan and quote too, so I'd use what I already know. My dad would be a bit offended, but he'd get over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to make that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five-a-side on Thursdays, probably, and the holiday Ana and I wanted in Portugal. That's fine. I'd rather give up a holiday now than a whole career later.

say: I'd say five years is enough **if people stop pretending**.
I'd tell the young warehouse lads to get a **trade ticket** now.
think: Five years is the **sweet spot** to finish an apprenticeship.
The desk work goes in 2031, but **plumbing hands** last until about 2034.
do: Apply for the **adult plumbing apprenticeship**, two days a week.
Ask Ferro to keep him on **three days** and use AI to cover the work.
Build savings up to **four months** of bills.
feel: **Busy-anxious**, steadier because he has a plan.
S3.quote: I'd rather give up a holiday now than a whole career later.
fieldNote: He picks plumbing because he knows it from the **paperwork side** at Ferro.
He'd use AI to **shrink his desk hours** while he trains.
A **clear plan** lowers his distress compared with the 2-year card.

steps.text: Apply for the college's adult plumbing apprenticeship, two days weekly
Use AI tools to fit Ferro work into three days
Grow savings from three to four months of bills
Drop five-a-side and cancel the Portugal holiday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so let's be sensible about it. People at work would probably relax completely, and I'd be the boring one telling them to plan. That's fine, I don't mind being boring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes me calmer about my own plans. I'd be thirty-seven when it lands, with time to have a trade, maybe a family, and a few years of savings. The risk is that everyone waits and the apprenticeships fill up at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Ferro for a couple more years and get really good with the AI tools, because that's money now. Around year three I'd start the plumbing apprenticeship, and I'd open a pension top-up so I'm not relying on anyone later. We'd get engaged on the normal timeline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not scared. It's a long road with a known end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said everyone waits. Are you sure you won't wait too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'm not sure. I'm steady, not a go-getter, and steady people wait. So I'd write the start date for the apprenticeship on the kitchen calendar where Ana can see it and nag me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your kids to study, if you have them by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my kids to learn something with their hands and something with their heads, both. My dad gave me the hands and the college gave me the head. In ten years you'd need both to stay in work.

say: I'd say there's **time**, so let's be sensible.
I'd be the **boring one** at work telling people to plan.
think: Ten years makes me **calmer** about my own plans.
The danger is everyone waits and **apprenticeships fill up** at the end.
do: Stay at Ferro and get **really good** with AI tools for now.
Start the **plumbing apprenticeship** around year three.
Open a **pension top-up** and get engaged on the normal timeline.
feel: **Uneasy**, not scared, about a long road with a known end.
S4.quote: My dad gave me the hands and the college gave me the head.
fieldNote: He openly admits **steady people wait**, and builds in a reminder.
He spots a **crowding risk** for apprenticeships near the deadline.
Family is central: he'd still **get engaged** on schedule.

steps.text: Master Ferro's AI ordering and van-planning tools over two years
Write the apprenticeship start date on the kitchen calendar
Open a monthly pension top-up alongside the workplace scheme
Propose to Ana on the original timeline next year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be starting a trade from scratch with the desk already gone and Ana paying the bills. What would help is a paid apprenticeship for adults, so I could learn plumbing without our savings running dry. Grants for training, not benefits, is what I'd want.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked what I'd tell the bosses at Ferro. I'd tell them to keep a person who knows the customers, because a van that turns up at the wrong site costs more than my wage. Machines are fine until something goes wrong.

headlineQuote: A van that turns up at the wrong site costs more than my wage.
portrait: Diego is a **27-year-old** admin at a plumbing wholesaler, scheduling vans and raising purchase orders.
He uses AI **now and then** and would move toward the tools as change speeds up.
His **plasterer father** and nurse girlfriend Ana are his safety nets and his sense of duty.
With faster AGI, he'd switch to a **hands-on trade**, using the three-year robot gap.
He wants **paid adult apprenticeships**, not benefits, and admits steady people tend to wait.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, starting a trade from scratch with his desk job already gone.
Having **Ana pay the bills** while he retrains.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid adult apprenticeship** so retraining doesn't drain savings.
